A portable panel delivers about 70–80% of its rated watts in real sun (Jackery's own figure; Goal Zero and Anker say the same without a number), so a 200 W panel gives about 140 W and needs seven hours of strong sun for 1,000 Wh, a 400 W panel about 3.6 hours.  How the hours are computed: hours = 1,000 Wh ÷ (rated W × 0.7).  Voltage first, watts second. The panel's open-circuit voltage (Voc, cold morning, no load) must sit inside the station's input range. Panels in series add their Voc; in parallel they add current, so check the amp limit too.
 Connectors. MC4 is the common ground (ALLPOWERS, EcoFlow, BLUETTI, Anker's cables terminate in XT60); Jackery uses DC8020, Goal Zero its HPP plug, DJI a proprietary plug that needs the adapter module.  A station-and-panel combination only works if three things line up: the panel's total wattage sits at or under the station's published maximum solar input, the connector matches, and the panel's voltage is inside the station's accepted range. Get the first wrong and you have paid for watts the station will refuse. Get the second or third wrong and nothing charges at all. Here is each pairing in our registry with the arithmetic done. 
 Match the panel to the published input, not to the battery
 The instinct is to size the panel against the battery - a 1kWh battery, so a 1kW of panel. That is the wrong number. Every station publishes a maximum solar input, and that figure is set by its charge controller, not by its cells. The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 publishes 400W. Point 800W of panel at it and 400W of that panel is doing nothing.

 Two stations are missing from that table on purpose. Jackery publishes no maximum solar input for the Explorer 300 or for the Explorer 2000 v2, and EcoFlow publishes none for the DELTA Pro 3 in its overview. Those are blanks in the manufacturers' own specifications and we will not fill them in - which also means we cannot responsibly recommend a panel pairing for any of the three. 
 What a panel actually delivers
 A panel's rating is measured under standard test conditions: a specific irradiance, a specific cell temperature, a specific spectrum. Outdoors, in real sun, at a real angle, on a real day, you get less - and the shortfall is not small. The convention this site uses is 75% of nameplate as a good-conditions working figure, which is deliberately conservative, and you should expect well below that in haze, through glass, in winter, or with the panel lying flat instead of aimed. 
 Filling a 1,070Wh Jackery from two 200W panels
 Two SolarSaga 200W panels = 400W of nameplate 
 At 75% in good conditions = 300W actual 
 1,070Wh at 85% usable = 910Wh to replace 
 910Wh / 300W = about 3.0 hours of good sun 
 In haze or at a poor angle, call it 150W: 6.1 hours 
 Three hours of strong sun, or most of a mediocre day. That is the useful shape of the answer: a matched pair of 200W panels refills this unit daily in summer, and keeps pace with a moderate draw rather than refilling it in winter. 
 The connector is where combinations go wrong
 Jackery panels terminate in Jackery's own DC connector. The EcoFlow 220W Bifacial uses photovoltaic MC4-style connectors. Anker publishes an XT60i solar input on the C1000 Gen 2 and the C2000 Gen 2. These are not interchangeable without an adapter lead, and an adapter has to be right about more than the plug shape - the station publishes an acceptable input voltage window, and a panel outside it will either not charge or charge at a fraction of its rating. 
 This is the practical argument for buying the pair from one brand even when a mixed set looks cheaper. It is also why our registry carries panels from two brands only: we will not recommend a pairing we cannot verify the connector on. Best portable solar panels for power stations covers the panels themselves in detail, and how much solar input do you need works the sizing from the other direction. 
 Is a bundle actually cheaper?
 Often, and that is the honest reason the combination exists as a product: manufacturers discount the kit against the parts, and a kit arrives with the correct lead in the box. What a bundle also does is decide your panel wattage for you, frequently at the low end - a 1kWh station bundled with a single 100W panel will take most of two good days to fill, which is not what the buyer imagined. 
 So read the bundle's panel wattage against the station's published input ceiling before you treat the discount as a saving. A kit at half the input ceiling is fine if you plan to add panels; it is a disappointment if you expected the kit to be the finished system. And if the word 'solar generator' is what brought you here, portable power station vs solar generator clears up what is mostly a naming problem - a solar generator is a power station with a panel in the box. 
 Bifacial panels only pay on the right ground
 EcoFlow publishes 220W on the front of its bifacial panel and 175W on the rear. That rear figure is real, and it is worth genuine watts on snow, dry sand or light gravel, where reflected light reaches the back face. On grass, dark soil or asphalt it contributes very little. Buy bifacial for a winter or desert setup; on a green campsite you are paying for a face that is looking at nothing.

Best Solar Panels for Each Popular Power Station: Matched by Connector, Voltage, and Watts | StormWatts Skip to content Disclosure: Some links that go through stormwatts.com/go/ are affiliate links (currently BLUETTI and EcoFlow via Awin, and Anker SOLIX via Rakuten Advertising). If you buy through one, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. It never changes what we recommend. Links for brands that haven’t approved us go straight to their official page with no tracking. How we make money . AI-assisted research: this page was researched and written with AI assistance from manufacturers’ official spec pages and manuals and government sources (linked below). We have not tested these products hands-on. Methodology . Short answer: for most popular power stations, the best panel is the brand’s own panel wired exactly the way the brand shows. That’s mainly because the connector and voltage already match. What the brand pages don’t tell you is how close some of those setups run to the voltage limit on a cold morning, or how far they fall short of the station’s solar cap. Using each brand’s published specs (all checked October 20, 2026), we found:
 Several stations can’t reach their solar cap with the brand’s own portable panels. The biggest gaps: the Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus accepts 1,400 W but tops out around 1,000 W with two SolarSaga 500 X panels, and the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 accepts 2,600 W, but four EcoFlow 400W panels wired the cold-safe way give 1,600 W . The DELTA 3 Plus (800 W of 1,000 W) and BLUETTI AC180 (400 W of 500 W with the panels on BLUETTI’s US store) fall short by less.
 EcoFlow’s own manual shows three 400W panels in series (144 V) on the DELTA Pro 3’s 150 V input. Using EcoFlow’s published temperature coefficient, our math puts that string over 150 V whenever the panels are colder than about 54°F . That’s fine in July and a problem on a sunny winter morning. EcoFlow support told StormWatts by email on Oct 22, 2026 that the diagram “is an example based on standard electrical parameters and does not apply to all climate conditions,” and recommended two panels in series on High-PV plus the third on Low-PV for cold climates.
 Anker’s PS200 panel has a 57.6 V open-circuit voltage, and the C1000 Gen 2 accepts up to 60 V. That leaves about 4% headroom at 77°F, and Anker doesn’t publish how much the panel’s voltage rises in the cold. Anker support confirmed that by email on Oct 22, 2026 and advised monitoring the panel’s Voc and not exceeding 60 V in sub-freezing weather.
 Jackery support told StormWatts by email on Oct 22, 2026 not to put three SolarSaga 200W panels in series on one Explorer 2000 Plus input , because the string exceeds the 60 V limit.
 The full station-by-station picks are below, followed by a cross-brand chart showing how many 200W-class panels from each brand fit each station.
 Safety first. Exceeding a power station’s input voltage can damage it. Use the voltage limits in your unit’s manual, keep cold-weather margin, and don’t mix panel models on one input. Never backfeed a house through a wall outlet; hardwired loads need a transfer switch or inlet installed by a licensed electrician ( transfer switch guide ). This page is research from manufacturer documents, not electrical advice.
 How we matched panels to stations
 These are the same four checks from our solar panel compatibility guide , applied to specific panels:
 Connector. Does the panel plug in directly, or do you need an adapter? Brand panels usually include the right cable; mixing brands usually means buying one.
 Voltage window. In series , panel voltages add. The string’s open-circuit voltage ( Voc ) must stay under the station’s maximum, and its working voltage ( Vmp ) must stay above the station’s minimum. In parallel , voltage stays the same and currents add.
 Cold-weather Voc. Voc goes up when panels are cold. We checked every string at −4°F (−20°C) , a realistic sunny winter morning in the Upper Midwest, and also at 14°F (−10°C).
 Amps and watts. Parallel strings must stay under the input’s current limit, and the total panel watts should land near the station’s solar cap without going far past it.
 Our math, labeled as ours: 
 Cold Voc ≈ panel Voc × panels in series × (1 + temperature coefficient × (25°C − panel temperature))
 Where a brand publishes a voltage temperature coefficient, we use it: Jackery SolarSaga 200W −0.27%/°C, SolarSaga 100 Air −0.25%/°C, SolarSaga 500 X −0.26%/°C, EcoFlow 400W −0.33%/°C.
 Assumption: EcoFlow’s 220W, Anker’s PS200/PS400, and BLUETTI’s panels have no published coefficient on the pages we checked, so we use −0.33%/°C , the steepest coefficient published among the panels in this guide. Your panel’s label may differ.
 Panel ratings also carry a ±5% Voc tolerance (Jackery and Anker print it). We don’t add that on top, but it’s another reason to leave headroom.
 Refill times use the 85% solar charge-path efficiency assumption and peak sun hours method from our solar panel count guide .
 We have not tested any of these panels. Prices are what each brand’s official US store listed on October 20, 2026, and they change often.

Station-plus-panel bundles are often cheaper; see solar generator bundles vs buying separately . “Peak-sun hours to refill” is from empty at the panels’ rated watts (capped at the station’s limit) × 85%. Compare it with your local sun hours from NREL’s PVWatts .
 Notes on each match
 Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 and 2000 v2: two SolarSaga 200W, one per input
 Both stations have two DC 8mm inputs and a combined 400 W solar cap. The 1000 v2 lists 16–60 V at 10.5 A per input; the 2000 v2 lists 16–60 V at 12 A ( 1000 v2 , 2000 v2 ). The SolarSaga 200W on Jackery’s current listing is 22 V Voc, 18 V / 11.5 A at full output, −0.27%/°C, 60 V maximum system voltage , with a DC8020 cable and a DC8020-to-DC7909 adapter in the box ( SolarSaga 200W , $379, list $429).
 Two panels reach the 400 W cap. A third adds nothing at peak.
 One quirk on the 1000 v2 (our math): the panel’s rated current (11.5 A) is above that model’s 10.5 A per-input limit. The station simply draws less, so one panel per input tops out near 18 V × 10.5 A ≈ 190 W at the rated point. Real-world output is usually below the rating anyway, so this rarely matters.
 The 2000 v2 problem isn’t the panels; it’s the cap. Twice the battery on the same 400 W input means about 6 peak sun hours for a full refill, more than a typical winter day.
 Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus: 1,000 W is the practical ceiling with Jackery panels
 The 2000 Plus has two DC 8mm inputs rated 17.5–60 V (working voltage), 12 A each, 24 A / 1,400 W combined . That’s the same on Jackery’s product page and in the Explorer 2000 Plus user manual (model JE-2000C) ( product page ). Jackery’s store now points shoppers to the newer HomePower 2000 Plus v2, and the 2000 Plus listing showed kit and refurbished variants on October 20.
 SolarSaga 500 X, one per input: 1,000 W. Jackery’s spec for the 500 X is 48.5 V Voc, 41.7 V / 12.0 A at full output, 13.02 A short-circuit, −0.26%/°C (panel spec section of the Explorer 2000 Plus page ). It’s six 85 W panels that Jackery says must be wired in parallel only, never in series , and Jackery lists it as compatible with the 2000 Plus ( SolarSaga 500 X , $799, list $999). Our math: 54.2 V at −4°F, under 60 V. At 12.0 A, each panel sits right at the 12 A per-input limit, so two 500 X panels are the most this station can use , about 71% of the 1,400 W cap.
 Four SolarSaga 200W, two in series per input: 800 W. The manual says one or two panels plug straight into the inputs. For three or four panels it uses a solar series connector sold separately (listed as the Jackery Solar Panel Connector , $69, which Jackery says joins two or three panels in series). The manual also requires the same panel type and the same number of panels on both inputs and shows uneven setups (2+1, 3+1, 3+2) as prohibited.
 What about six 200W panels? Jackery’s product page advertises “Fast Solar Charge in 2 Hours with Solar Panel 200W*6”, and the manual’s diagram shows three SolarSaga panels per input. On paper, three SolarSaga 200W in series have a Voc of 66 V at 77°F (74.4 V for the JS-200D version below). That’s above the 60 V top of the station’s published input range and above the 60 V maximum system voltage printed on both SolarSaga 200 spec sheets. Jackery rates this input by working voltage (three panels’ Vmp is about 54–60 V), not by a maximum Voc, and we couldn’t reconcile the two from Jackery’s published documents. Jackery’s answer (email to StormWatts, Oct 22, 2026): “Please do not connect three SolarSaga 200W panels in series to one DC input port,” because the panel’s 24.8 V ±5% Voc puts a three-panel string over the station’s 60 V limit, which “may prevent charging or cause product damage.” Jackery said each port takes up to three panels, both ports need the same model and number of panels, six panels is the maximum, and for six SolarSaga 200W it said to “combine three panels with one adapter” (the SolarSaga Adapter for Pro/Plus/New Series) on each input. In a follow-up email on Oct 27, 2026, Jackery said its Solar Panel Connector “connects the panels in series” and that each input “supports connecting two SolarSaga 200W panels in series” but not three. On Oct 28, 2026, Jackery support reversed itself in a third email: it said the “SolarSaga Adapter” is “the exact same product as our ‘Solar Panel Connector’” (a translation mix-up), that Jackery doesn’t make a three-panel parallel connector, and that “you CAN safely connect three SolarSaga 200W panels in series per port on the Explorer 2000 Plus,” because “the 60V limit in the manual is actually a conservative safety buffer” and three panels’ working voltage is “right around 60V.” Jackery called this “a special exception for our Pro and Plus series models.” We can’t square that with the printed 17.5–60 V input range, the 60 V maximum system voltage on the panel label, or Jackery’s own Oct 22 and Oct 27 answers: three in series is about 74 V open-circuit at 77°F and higher in the cold, and the station sees open-circuit voltage before it starts drawing power. Jackery hasn’t published the higher limit. So our rule for this station is unchanged: two SolarSaga 200W in series per input (four panels, about 800 W) fits Jackery’s published limits. If you want three per input, get Jackery to confirm it in writing for your unit and warranty first. If the panels sit far from the station, run the extension after the series connector; see solar extension cables and voltage drop .
 Jackery’s successor, the HomePower 2000 Plus v2, caps solar input at 800 W (vs 1,400 W here); see v2 vs Explorer 2000 Plus: solar input compared .
 EcoFlow’s new DELTA 3000 and 3800 Gen4 (not shipping yet as of Nov 5) use a different solar port: LP60, 11–60 V, 20 A, 1,000 W each. See what panels fit the Gen4 port .
 BLUETTI’s new Apex 200 (US launch pricing live Nov 5–6) takes up to 3,000 W across XT60 12–60 V and MC4 60–280 V ports—see Apex 200 solar input and panel fit .
 Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus: SolarSaga 500 X, one per input
 Two DC8020 inputs, 16–60 V, 12 A each, 1,000 W combined . Jackery’s FAQ says to keep panel open-circuit voltage within that range and recommends Jackery panels ( FAQ ). Two 500 X panels hit the 1,000 W cap exactly, at $1.60 per panel watt ($1,598).
 The other route is four SolarSaga 200W, two in series per input: 800 W for $1,516 before connectors. However, the HomePower 3600 Plus isn’t on the compatibility list of Jackery’s $69 series connector, so check with Jackery first. Jackery’s own HomePower 3600 Plus + 2 × SolarSaga 200W kit is 400 W, 40% of the cap.
 EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus: two EcoFlow 400W, one per input
 The DELTA 3 Plus has two XT60i inputs, each 11–60 V, 15 A, 500 W (1,000 W total). The manual says to keep the panels’ total Voc within 60 V and total short-circuit current (Isc) within 15 A on each input, using EcoFlow’s Solar-to-XT60i cable ( user manual ).
 EcoFlow 400W, one per input: 800 W. EcoFlow’s manual lists 48 V Voc (41 V working), 11 A Isc (9.8 A working), MC4, −0.33%/°C ( 400W panel manual ). Our math: 55.1 V at −4°F. Two in series (96 V) is far over 60 V, so it’s one per input. $699 each or $1,099 for two ($1.37/W) on October 20 ( EcoFlow ).
 Four NextGen 220W Bifacial, two in series per input: 880 W. The 220W lists 21.5 V Voc (18.4 V working), 12.4 A Isc ( EcoFlow ). Two in series is 43 V (49.4 V at −4°F, assumed coefficient). Two in parallel would be 24.8 A Isc, over the 15 A rule. It’s slightly more watts than the 400W pair but costs $1,538 (two 2-packs at $769), so the 400W pair is the better value.
 EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3: four 400W panels, and a warning about EcoFlow’s own diagram
 The DELTA Pro 3 has a High-PV XT60 input (30–150 V, 15 A, 1,600 W) and a Low-PV XT60i input (11–60 V, 20 A, 1,000 W) . Its manual says overvoltage protection handles up to 155 V on High-PV and 62 V on Low-PV, warns that “Voc can fluctuate with temperature changes,” and shows EcoFlow 400W panels as an example: three in series on High-PV (144 V) and two in parallel on Low-PV (48 V, 19.6 A) ( user manual ).
 Our math with EcoFlow’s published −0.33%/°C coefficient for that panel:
 High-PV string of EcoFlow 400W Voc at 77°F Crosses 150 V input limit below Crosses 155 V protection limit below At −4°F 
 2 in series 96 V Never in normal weather Never in normal weather ≈ 110 V 
 3 in series (EcoFlow’s diagram) 144 V ≈ 54°F panel temperature ≈ 35°F ≈ 165 V 
 Panels heat up once they’re producing power, but open-circuit voltage is highest at dawn, when cold panels see first light before the station starts drawing current. For year-round use in a cold climate, we’d run two 400W panels in series on High-PV (800 W) plus EcoFlow’s two-in-parallel Low-PV setup (800 W). That’s 1,600 W from four panels ($2,099 for EcoFlow’s 4-pack on October 20), about 62% of the 2,600 W cap. EcoFlow itself notes that reaching 2,600 W “may require the use of higher-power solar panels” ( product page FAQ ).
 What EcoFlow said (support email to StormWatts, Oct 22, 2026, case CAS-20261022-2098456): the three-in-series diagram “is an example based on standard electrical parameters and does not apply to all climate conditions,” and “in low-temperature environments, the series Voc should be recalculated according to the minimum expected local temperature.” For cold-climate users with three 400W panels, EcoFlow recommended two in series on High-PV and the third panel on Low-PV , so the third panel’s output isn’t lost. EcoFlow didn’t point us to a published derating table. With a fourth panel, our four-panel layout above (2 in series on High-PV, 2 in parallel on Low-PV) follows the same idea.
 Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2: Anker’s three-panel setup has almost no voltage headroom on paper
 The C1000 Gen 2 has one XT60i solar input. Its product page lists “600W MAX; 11-60V, 14.5A” (checked Oct 20), and the user guide splits that into 11–28 V at 8.2 A and 28–60 V at 14.5 A ( user guide , checked Oct 16). Anker’s guidance for the full 600 W is 6 × 100 W, 3 × 200 W, or 400 W + 200 W, with input voltage at or below 60 V when panels are wired in parallel ( C1000 Gen 2 , guidance checked Oct 7).
 Anker’s own panel: Anker’s support spec page for the PS200 lists 57.6 V open-circuit, 48 V / 4.16 A operating, 4.35 A short-circuit ( Anker support ). The current PS200 Bifacial page lists the same 48 V ⎓ 4.16 A output and includes an XT-60i cable ($499.99 on October 20, Anker ).
 Three in parallel gives 48 V × 12.5 A ≈ 600 W, under the 14.5 A limit. That’s Anker’s recommended setup and the best wattage match.
 The catch (our math): 57.6 V leaves only 2.4 V (about 4%) below the 60 V input limit at 77°F. Anker doesn’t publish the PS200’s temperature coefficient. With any coefficient typical of the panels in this guide (−0.25% to −0.33%/°C), the panel’s open-circuit voltage would pass 60 V somewhere around 47–54°F . Anker sells these panels for this station, so its input may tolerate more than the published 60 V (EcoFlow, for example, publishes 62 V protection on its 60 V inputs), but Anker’s pages don’t say so. Anker’s answer (support email to StormWatts, Oct 22, 2026, ticket ANKER-TNX8721417221): the PS200’s 57.6 V is within the C1000 Gen 2’s 11–60 V range, but “cold-weather voltage rise could push the Voc closer to the upper limit”; Anker “does not publish a specific temperature coefficient for the PS200,” and it recommends monitoring the panel’s Voc in sub-freezing temperatures and avoiding going over 60 V. Anker didn’t say its input tolerates more than 60 V. If you’ll charge below freezing, we’d use the lower-voltage option below instead. The 400 W + 200 W option (about $1,200 with a PS400) has the same 57.6 V Voc.
 Lower-voltage alternative: two ~22–25 V panels in series (about 400–440 W) stay well under 60 V in the cold. See the cross-brand chart below; they’ll need an MC4-to-XT60i cable.
 Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus: eight PS400s in Anker’s 2S2P layout
 The F3800 Plus has two independent inputs, each 11–165 V, 17 A, 1,600 W . Anker’s product page warns that “exceeding 165V may cause damage to the solar input ports” ( F3800 Plus ; also in the user guide ). Anker replaced XT60 on this model with its own high-voltage plug, saying XT60 connectors “aren’t suitable for high-voltage PV systems.” Its High-Voltage Solar Charging Cable (Anker plug to MC4, 20 A) was $34.99 on October 20.
 Anker’s F3800 Plus Technical Brief and Design Guide (V1.1, June 2025) supports 2 in series, 2 in parallel (2S2P) per input with its 400W portable panels (48 V / 8.3 A), and up to four rigid 405 W panels in series per input. Anker’s PS400 spec page lists 57.6 V open-circuit, 48 V / 8.33 A operating ( Anker support ).
 2S2P × 2 inputs = 8 panels, 3,200 W. Our math: 115.2 V per string at 77°F, about 132 V at −4°F (assumed coefficient), under 165 V. Current is 16.7 A per input at full output, just under 17 A. Eight PS400 Bifacial panels were $5,599.92 ($699.99 each) on October 20, plus two HV cables and parallel connectors.
 Three in series won’t work with these panels: 172.8 V at 77°F, already over 165 V.
 Rigid 440W panels: Anker support told StormWatts by email on Oct 22, 2026 that four 440W rigid panels in series (about 156.6 V at 77°F) are within 165 V, but that “it is safer to use three panels in series per input port, especially in sub-freezing conditions” (details in portable vs rigid panels ).
 Something to watch in Anker’s guide: it sizes series strings by operating voltage (165 V ÷ 31.18 V ≈ 5.29 panels). Open-circuit voltage is higher than operating voltage, and higher still in the cold, so always check a string against Voc , not Vmp.
 Half-size option: four PS400s (2 in series per input) give 1,600 W for $2,799.96, about 2.8 peak sun hours to refill the 3,840 Wh battery (our math).
 BLUETTI AC180: two BLUETTI 200W panels in series
 BLUETTI lists the AC180’s solar input as 500 W max, Voc 12–60 V, 10 A and requires panels with MC4 connectors. It recommends 1 × PV420, 1 × PV350, or 2 × PV200 ( AC180 ). On October 20, the panels we could find on BLUETTI’s US store were the 200W SP200L and a 350W panel.
 2 × BLUETTI 200W (SP200L) in series: 400 W. BLUETTI lists 24.6 V open-circuit, 10.8 A short-circuit, MC4 , and says not to mix panel models ( SP200L , $399 or $798 for two on Oct 20; the single panel was on sale for $349 on Oct 24, 2026). Our math: 49.2 V at 77°F, about 56.5 V at −4°F (assumed coefficient), under 60 V. Three in series (73.8 V) is over. The listing also showed a shipping notice, so check availability.
 BLUETTI 350W: less than it sounds on the AC180. BLUETTI lists a 33 V open-circuit voltage ( 350W panel , $649). Our math: even if the panel ran at its full 33 V, the AC180’s 10 A limit caps it at 33 V × 10 A = 330 W , and real operating voltage is lower than Voc. So expect noticeably under 330 W from one panel. Two in series (66 V) are over the limit, and two in parallel exceed 10 A.

 Our math, using the rules above: cold Voc at −4°F must stay at or under 60 V, a string’s working voltage must clear the station’s minimum, parallel strings must stay under the input’s current limit, and total panel watts can’t exceed the station’s cap by more than 10%. This is electrical fit only . Mixing brands also means buying an adapter cable, and brands may not support it. Jackery’s manual, for example, says it “will not be responsible for the losses caused by using other brands’ solar panels.”

 Write down your station’s input voltage range, current limit per input, watt cap, and connector (table above, then confirm in the manual).

 In series, multiply Voc by the number of panels and add the cold-weather rise for your coldest sunny morning. In parallel, add the currents.

results.title: In Some Ways, Bluetti's Step-Down Apex 200 is a Step Up From the Apex 300
results.snippet: Bluetti’s Apex 200 trades some of the Apex 300’s power and whole-home capabilities for greater portability and versatility. At 59 pounds and about 28 percent smaller than the 84-pound Apex 300, it is better suited to road trips and RV use while still offering useful home backup. It delivers 3,200 watts continuously and has a 2,560Wh battery; the reviewer ran a refrigerator for 27 hours and estimated efficiency above 90 percent. Built-in USB and 12-volt outputs, plus app-controlled individual AC outlets, improve its usefulness on the go. It lacks 240-volt output, so it cannot support high-voltage appliances or advanced whole-home backup. Like the Apex 300, it supports battery expansion and passthrough charging, and can pair with the 300 for more than 7,000 watts of output. Its standout feature is up to 3,000 watts of solar input through separate low- and high-voltage connections, enabling rapid recharging in ideal conditions. The Apex 200 is best for travelers and overlanders who also want limited 120-volt emergency backup.

 Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us? 
 4 min read 
 When I reviewed the Bluetti Apex 300 power station earlier this year, I was impressed with how powerful it was and how easy it was to expand into a robust home backup system. But there were a few notable trade-offs, mostly in portability and a lower variety of outlets. With Bluetti’s Apex 200 power station , those drawbacks are answered with a powerful model that’s much better suited to life on the road.
 Physically, it’s not hard to notice the difference between the two units. At 84 pounds, the Apex 300 is large and heavy to tote around. The 200 is 59 pounds and roughly 28 percent smaller. It’s not as powerful as its larger sibling, but the 200 is still definitely built for use in the home, while being more adaptable for long road trips or cross-country treks in an RV.

 Key Specs

 Capacity 2,560 Wh 
 Max Solar Input 3,000 W 
 Outlets 3 x 120V; 1 x 120V 30A; 2 x USB-C, 2 x USB-A; 1 x 12V; 1 x 12V 30A 
 Weight 59 lb 
 Good for Basic Home Backup or Road Trips
 The Apex 200 outputs up to 3,200 watts of continuous power (it says 3,600 on the front, but that’s only if it’s connected to an expansion battery ). That’s enough to run several appliances or even a few circuits in your home electrical system if you connect it to a manual transfer switch using the 120-volt, 30-amp port. It also has a 2,560-watt-hour capacity, which can provide several hours of power—I ran my refrigerator for a full 27 hours on a single charge, and when I ran the numbers, I estimated that it runs just over 90 percent efficiently, which is very good for a power station.
 Trevor Raab The front panel is angled, making the display easier to read from above. It features both AC and direct DC output, and has a 120-volt 30-amp outlet for connecting to a transfer switch of an RV.
 The 200 also brings direct DC power back, with a bank of USB outlets and both 10- and 30-amp 12-volt outputs. This is something the Apex 300 doesn’t have built-in (it requires an optional hub to add it), which makes it a bit less versatile as a portable station.
 One niche feature I really liked was the ability to turn off each AC outlet individually using the mobile app. Doing this helps to cut down on the slight battery drain that an idle outlet can contribute, and it’s not commonly seen on power stations. It might seem like a small thing, but when you’re trying to get the most runtime out of your power station, every little bit helps. It’s also handy if you want to turn off power to one device, but not another.
 Trevor Raab A cool feature is the ability to turn individual AC outlets on and off, which helps prevent battery drain from outlets not in use. Or you can turn off devices plugged into it remotely over Wi-Fi.
 What you don’t get with the Apex 200, however, is 240-volt output for higher-powered applications like powering high-voltage appliances or HVAC systems. That means it’s not suited for advanced whole-home backup like the Apex 300 is, but it's fine if you're only powering 120-volt appliances.
 The Apex 200 does, however, mimic the modularity of the 300. You can add up to six additional batteries to expand your capacity to over 33 kilowatt-hours using the largest batteries Bluetti offers, the B500K . You can also pair it with the Apex 300 to combine and increase total power output to over 7,000 watts.
 Solar Charging Game Changer
 One of the most surprising features I found with the Apex 200 was a maximum solar input of up to 3,000 watts. That’s incredibly high for a power station in this size range. It achieves this by offering two sets of inputs: low-voltage XT60 input (up to 1,000 watts) and high-voltage MC4 input (up to 2,000 watts). If you had the rated panels to support both of these inputs, you could fully recharge this station in just a few hours on a perfectly sunny day.
 Trevor Raab The Apex 300 has a high-voltage solar input (bottom left), which helps it achieve 3,000 watts of max solar input. That’s not common in power stations of this size.
 This attention to detail on solar recharging makes the Apex 200 one of the most robust power stations I’ve seen targeted to the on-the-go end user who likes to tap into the sun's rays for energy while off-grid and on the road. Of course, it also features standard charging from AC power, including a Turbo mode that supports fast charging, an auto mode that allows you to set the rate you prefer, or a silent mode that limits the amount of input so that the cooling fan doesn’t need to turn on (which on this model can be a bit loud).
 Another feature I like is passthrough charging, which allows you to run devices from the station while recharging the battery at the full rate. The inverters in lesser power stations will throttle the input if they need to power something at the same time, but not here. This is true of the Apex 300, too, and I’m glad they kept this feature in the Apex 300.
 Who Is the Apex 200 Best For?
 For my money, this power station is best suited to those who plan to use the Apex 200 for limited home backup during emergencies to power 120-volt devices or circuits, while also wanting to take it on trips. Overlanders, especially, will appreciate the lighter weight and portability, and they’ll also love the high solar input, which can come in handy when you’re on the road and out of range of AC power. I still like the Apex 300 a lot, but the Apex 200 shows that a bit more versatility can go a long way.

Power Station Solar Input Explained: Voc, Watts, Amps | Amphourly Skip to content On this page Key takeaways
 A panel fits a power station when its open-circuit voltage (Voc) sits inside the station's solar input window and the connector matches, directly or with an adapter.
 Most stations we track top out at 55-60 V; small units cap at 27-35 V, and a handful of large ones accept 145-165 V for long series strings.
 Too-high Voc can damage the charge controller; too-low Voc means the station may never start charging.
 A station's solar watt rating is a cap, not a promise: we assume panels deliver 75% of their rating, and the station clips anything above its limit.
 Cold raises Voc. Three 48 V panels in series (144 V) look safe on a 150 V input at 25°C but can exceed it on a frosty morning.
 A power station’s solar input voltage is the range of panel voltages it accepts, such as 11-60 V or 12-28 V. Your panel’s open-circuit voltage (Voc) must sit inside that window, with margin for cold weather, and its plug must match the port. The station’s watt rating is a ceiling: it takes up to that much and clips the rest.
 We pulled the solar input specs for every station in our power station database to show what those windows look like in practice, and how our solar panel matcher flags panels that would over-volt or under-perform.
 What do Voc, Vmp and Isc mean?
 Every panel spec sheet lists four electrical numbers. Two are voltages, two are currents:

 Three things stand out. Small stations almost all cap at 27-35 V, so they need 12 V-class panels. The big 1-2 kWh middle of the market sits at 55-60 V, which accepts nearly any single portable panel. And a handful of large stations accept high voltage, which lets you run long series strings with thinner cables.
 Some stations split those numbers across two ports. EcoFlow’s DELTA Pro 3 spec table lists a high-voltage port (30-150 V) and a low-voltage port (11-60 V), so match each panel string to the right port. The DELTA 3 Plus has two 11-60 V inputs at 500 W each, per its spec table .
 The connector is the other half of fit. Most stations we track use XT60 or the pin-compatible XT60i. Jackery’s 1 kWh-plus Explorers and the Goal Zero Yeti 500 use 8 mm DC, the BLUETTI AC180 uses DC7909, a few use Anderson or a brand-specific plug, and several don’t publish one. MC4 panels connect to any of them through an adapter cable; our solar panel connectors guide covers each plug.

 What happens if solar panel voltage is too high for a power station? Exceeding the maximum input voltage can damage the station's charge controller. Many stations shut the input off to protect themselves, but you shouldn't rely on it. Keep Voc, including cold-weather rise, under the limit.

 What is the difference between Voc and Vmp? Voc is the voltage with nothing connected, the highest a panel produces. Vmp is the voltage at which it delivers maximum power under load. Check Voc against the station's maximum and Vmp against its minimum operating voltage.

 Day three of a campground stay, and the cooler is a fridge now. A folding panel leans against the picnic table, angled at the afternoon sun, and the little screen on the power station says the battery is climbing back up while the fridge keeps running. That quiet, fuel-free refill is what people mean by a solar generator, and it works the same way at home when a storm takes the power out for a few days.
 The best solar generator for most people is a 1,000 Wh class portable power station with a LiFePO4 battery and at least 200 W of folding solar panels, like the Jackery Solar Generator 1000 v2 kit or an EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus with a 220 W panel. Plan on one to two sunny days to refill it from 200 W of panels, and add more panels if you need power every day.
 Prices change often. Where we give a price, it’s the maker’s own store price we saw in October 2026; check the current price before you buy. Amazon prices may differ, and kit prices change with sales. 
 What is a solar generator?
 A “solar generator” is not a generator in the gas-engine sense. It’s a marketing name for two things sold together: a portable power station (a big lithium battery with an inverter, wall outlets, USB ports and a built-in solar charge controller) and one or more portable solar panels that plug into it. The panels make DC electricity, the station stores it, and the inverter turns it into normal household AC power. There is no engine, no fuel and no exhaust, which is why a power station can sit in your kitchen or tent while the panels stay outside in the sun.
 A gas generator is a different machine with different rules. The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) says to run a gas generator outside only, at least 20 feet from the house, and never in a garage, basement or porch, because of carbon monoxide. A solar kit has none of that risk, but it also makes far less energy per day, so the trade-off is quiet and safe versus fast and fuel-hungry.

 A 200 W panel makes 200 W only in lab conditions: 1,000 watts of sunlight per square meter hitting it straight on, with the solar cells at 77°F (25°C). That’s the “standard test conditions” rating every panel uses. Outdoors, the sun is weaker in the morning and evening, panels get hot, clouds pass, and some energy is lost in cables and in the station’s charger. So use this simple formula:

 Peak sun hours are the day’s sunlight squeezed into “full-sun” hours of 1,000 W per square meter.
 0.75 is our planning factor for losses. The National Laboratory of the Rockies (formerly NREL) uses 14% default losses in its PVWatts calculator for a fixed, well-aimed rooftop system (dirt, wiring, mismatch, small shading and more), and a DOE study of 75 federal solar systems called a performance ratio of about 85% a realistic expectation. Portable panels that are propped up by hand, get hot and charge a battery lose more, so we round down to 75%. It’s an estimate, not a promise.

It holds 1,024 Wh (LiFePO4, rated for 4,000 cycles to 80%), delivers 1,800 W (3,600 W surge), switches to battery in under 10 ms if the grid drops, and charges from the wall in 56 minutes. EcoFlow’s headline is a 70-minute full charge from solar, which needs close to the full 1,000 W of panels in strong sun. You can add an extra battery later. It’s sold without panels: EcoFlow’s NextGen 220W Bifacial panel (220 W front, 175 W rear, IP68, 15.4 lb) is a good match, and two of them fill the station in about a sunny day. The maker’s price was about $669 in October 2026 (station only).
 Good: huge solar input for its size; fast wall charging; expandable; 5-year warranty.
 Watch out: panels cost extra; at 27.6 lb it’s a little heavier than the Jackery.
 Best for: home outages where you want to refill fast between storms, and anyone who’ll add panels over time.
 Check the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus price on Amazon 
 Check the EcoFlow NextGen 220W panel price on Amazon 
 3. Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 + 200W panel: best for fast wall top-ups
 The C1000 Gen 2 has 1,024 Wh, the strongest inverter in this size here at 2,000 W (3,000 W surge), and charges from empty to full in 49 minutes in UltraFast mode (turned on in the app; Anker says the battery must be above 68°F). It weighs 24.9 lb, and Anker rates it for 4,000 cycles to 80%. Solar input is up to 600 W at 29–60 V. Anker’s “1.8 hour” solar figure assumes the full 600 W; with the single 200 W panel in this kit, plan on about a day and a half of good sun. Add Anker’s PS400 bifacial panel (400 W, 21.9 lb, 5-year warranty) and you’d be close to the 600 W maximum.
 Good: powerful 2,000 W output; very fast wall charging; panel included.
 Watch out: not expandable (Anker says the Gen 2 isn’t); fastest charging needs a warm battery; Anker’s page doesn’t name the battery chemistry (the Amazon listing says LiFePO4).
 Best for: homes with power most of the time that want a quick-charge backup plus a solar fallback.
 Check the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 solar kit price on Amazon 
 4. EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus + 110W panel: best small kit
 For phones, a laptop, LED lights, a fan or a router through an outage, the RIVER 3 Plus is a small, 10.4 lb station with 286 Wh (LiFePO4, rated by EcoFlow for 3,000 cycles to 80%), 600 W AC output (1,200 W surge) and three AC outlets. It switches over in under 10 ms, so it can sit between the wall and your modem as a small backup. Its 220 W solar input is more than the 110 W panel in this kit needs, and our estimate says that panel refills the station in about one day of decent sun (110 × 4.5 × 0.75 ≈ 370 Wh). Extra batteries take it to 858 Wh. The station alone was about $299 at EcoFlow in October 2026.
 Good: light; one-day solar refill; fast UPS switchover; expandable.
 Watch out: 286 Wh won’t run a full-size fridge for long; EcoFlow’s page doesn’t state a warranty length for this model.
 Best for: apartments, small campsites, a router and lights during outages.
 Check the EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus solar kit price on Amazon 
 5. Goal Zero Yeti 1500 (6th Gen): best for wet weather
 Goal Zero’s new 2026 Yeti is built for being outside. It’s rated IPX4 against splashing water, holds 1,505 Wh in a LiFePO4 battery rated for 4,000 cycles to 80%, and puts out 2,000 W (3,600 W surge) from four AC outlets. Solar input goes up to 900 W across two inputs, so it can drink a lot of sun on a good day. From the wall it reaches 80% in about 0.8 hours. At 52.75 lb it’s heavy for its capacity, and it’s sold without panels. Goal Zero’s price was $1,499.95 in October 2026, with a 5-year warranty. Don’t confuse it with the older Yeti 1500X, which uses an NMC battery.
 Good: splash resistance; 900 W solar input; 1.5 kWh; 5-year warranty.
 Watch out: heavy; panels extra; costs more per watt-hour than the EcoFlow or Jackery.
 Best for: base camps, boats at the dock, job sites and porches where rain happens.
 Check the Goal Zero Yeti 1500 price on Amazon 
 6. EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 + 400W panel: best for home backup
 The DELTA Pro 3 holds 4,096 Wh (LiFePO4, 4,000 cycles to 80%), gives 4,000 W (8,000 W surge) at 120 V or 240 V, and accepts up to 2,600 W of solar through a high-voltage and a low-voltage input. It weighs 113.5 lb, on wheels. This kit adds one EcoFlow 400 W panel (22.6% efficiency, IP68), worth about 1,350 Wh a day by our estimate: a start, but you’d need several panels to refill it daily. EcoFlow’s price for the station alone was about $2,799 in October 2026, with a 5-year warranty. To power house circuits directly, EcoFlow’s Smart Home Panel 2 must be installed by an electrician; never plug a power station into a wall outlet to “backfeed” the house.
 Good: big capacity; 240 V for well pumps and larger loads; huge solar input; expandable.
 Watch out: heavy and expensive; one 400 W panel only covers a third of a full refill per day; EcoFlow’s US store showed the 400 W panel sold out in October 2026.
 Best for: homeowners planning for days-long outages who’ll add panels and an installed transfer panel.
 Check the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 solar kit price on Amazon 
 Solar panels to add
 Most stations take more solar than their kit includes. Before you buy another panel, check two numbers on your station: the maximum solar watts and the voltage range of its solar input. Also check the plug: Jackery panels use Jackery’s DC8020 plug and Anker panels come with an XT-60i cable, so mixing brands usually means an adapter cable.

 How to choose a solar generator
 Start with what you’ll run. Add up the watts of what you need at the same time (the station’s AC output must cover it, plus start-up surge for fridges and pumps), and the watt-hours you need per day.
 Estimate run time honestly. Usable energy is about 85% of the battery rating after inverter losses. A 1,024 Wh station gives about 870 Wh, so a 60 W load runs roughly 14 hours (870 ÷ 60). That’s an estimate; real loads vary.
 Match panels to your daily use. Panel watts ≈ daily Wh ÷ (peak sun hours × 0.75). Use your winter sun hours if you’re planning for winter storms.
 Look at the solar input limit. A station that takes 1,000 W of solar can refill in an afternoon with enough panels; one that takes 400 W never can.
 Choose LiFePO4. Every station here uses lithium iron phosphate, rated for thousands of cycles. Our LiFePO4 vs lithium-ion guide explains why.
 Don’t count on a tax credit. There is no federal tax credit for portable power stations or portable solar kits in 2026; the home solar and battery credit (25D) ended on December 31, 2025. Some states and utilities have their own programs.
 Keep exploring
 Start with our hub on portable power stations , or jump to the best portable power stations overall, picks for home backup and camping , and what size power station you need . For the bigger picture, read about solar energy and off-grid energy , or browse every guide in portable power stations .
 Solar generator questions
 Is a solar generator the same as a portable power station?
 Almost. A solar generator is a portable power station sold together with solar panels. The station is the battery, inverter and outlets; the panels recharge it. Any power station with a solar input becomes a “solar generator” once you plug in compatible panels, so you can also buy the station first and add panels later.
 How long does it take to charge a solar generator with solar panels?
 Divide the battery size by what your panels make in a day. With our estimate (panel watts × peak sun hours × 0.75), one 200 W panel makes about 675 Wh on a 4.5-sun-hour day, so a 1,000 Wh station takes about a day and a half. Two panels cut that to about one sunny day. Winter days can take three or four times longer.
 Can a solar generator run a house?
 Not a whole house in the normal way. The average U.S. home used about 10,800 kWh in 2022 (EIA), roughly 30 kWh a day, far more than a portable kit can store or collect. A large station like the DELTA Pro 3 can run essentials (fridge, lights, internet, a well pump on 240 V) for a while, connected through a transfer panel or switch installed by a licensed electrician.
 Can I use a solar generator indoors?
 Yes, the power station itself has no engine or exhaust, so it’s safe to use inside; keep it dry, ventilated and away from heat. The panels go outside in the sun, with the cable run through a window or door gap. A gas generator is the opposite: CPSC says outdoors only, at least 20 feet from the house.
 Do solar panels charge a power station on cloudy days?
 A little. The Department of Energy notes clouds can cut direct sunlight by up to 100% under heavy cover, so output can drop to a small fraction of the panel’s rating. Plan on wall or car charging as your backup, and size panels for your season’s average sun, not the best day.

 How to charge a power station with solar panels
Plug in a panel whose connector matches the station's solar input, or use the maker's adapter cable, and keep the
 panels' open-circuit voltage under the input's top voltage on the coldest morning you expect. Then stop adding panels at
 the input's watt limit: beyond it, extra panels charge no faster in full sun. A station refills in its capacity divided by the
 watts coming in, so a 1,000 Wh station on 200 W takes at least 5 hours of full sun from empty.
 From each maker's published input limits and panel figures, with our own arithmetic; we have not tested these setups ourselves.

 Quickest refill from a maker panel: 2 × Jackery SolarSaga 500 X , 1 panel on each of its 2 solar inputs , about 2.7 h of full sun from empty ( the same at a 70% panel yield: the panels are big enough to hold the limit even then ). Cable: an Anderson-to-DC8020 solar cable .
 Lowest panel cost at the full input: 2 × EcoFlow NextGen 220W Bifacial , 1 panel on each of its 2 solar inputs , about 3.5 h at a 70% yield.
 Every panel on the Explorer 1000 v2 , with prices and the cold-morning check 
 The steps, in order
 Read the solar input's limits. The manual or spec table gives a voltage range (for example 12 to 60 V),
 a current (in amps) and a watt limit. The voltage range is the one that matters most: below its bottom the station does not
 start charging, and above its top it can be damaged. Our setup page for each station quotes the
 maker's own lines.
 Choose the panel watts. Aim at the input's watt limit, or a little above it so the input stays full for
 more of the day: panels give about 70% of their rating on a good day, which is the yield we plan with. Watts above the limit are
 wasted at midday. On 75 of the 119 stations we have setups for, the quickest setup uses more than one panel.
 Wire the panels for the input. Panels in series add their voltages; strings in parallel add their
 currents. Series suits a high-voltage input, parallel a low-voltage one with a higher current limit. Two panels that each
 fit can break a limit together, so check the whole array, not one panel.
 Check the coldest morning. A panel's open-circuit voltage (Voc) is printed for 25 °C and rises as it gets colder, by about
 0.25% to 0.35% per °C. EcoFlow's 400 W panel is rated 48 V open-circuit and reaches about 53.5 V on a
-10 °C (14 °F) morning; two in series reach 107 V, too much for a 60 V input. Across our setups, the cold check
 lowers or rules out 322 station-and-panel pairs that would pass on a mild day.
 Use the right cable. Panels end in MC4 plugs or their maker's own (Jackery's DC8020 or Anderson). Most
 stations take XT60 or XT60i; others take DC8020 (8 mm), XT90, Anderson, DC5521 or MC4. On 93 of the 119 stations, the quickest maker panel needs an adapter cable, and on 84 it comes
 from another maker than the station's.
 Place the panels. Face them square to the sun: in the US, toward the south, tilted up at about your
 latitude (steeper in winter, flatter in summer). A panel on its kickstand catches more if you turn it to follow the sun
 every two or three hours. Keep every cell out of shade: in a series string the same current runs through every panel, so a
 shadow across one cuts the whole string. Leave the station itself in the shade, since a hot station slows or stops charging.
 Plug in and check the input watts. Read the solar watts on the station's display or app. If it shows
 nothing, see why a station may not charge below.
 Series and parallel, drawn from real setups
 Each picture is a setup from our pages, drawn as it is wired. The setups use identical panels, which is what makers advise.
 Series: voltages add 2 × BLUETTI SORA 500 on the BLUETTI AC200L: 2 in series on the solar input; 1,000 W in. Two panels in one string, for the BLUETTI AC200L : twice the voltage, the current of one panel.
 Parallel: currents add 2 × EcoFlow 400W on the Aferiy P180: 2 in parallel on the solar input; 500 W in. Two strings side by side, for the Aferiy P180 : the voltage of one panel, twice the current, joined by an MC4 branch connector.
 How long it takes
Hours of full sun to refill = the station's watt-hours ÷ the watts coming in. The watts coming in are the lower of the panels'
 output and the input's limit. At the limit that is the fastest the station can refill; at a 70% panel yield it takes
 longer. A usable day holds four to six hours of full sun in most of the US. In December a panel tilted for winter gets about
2.5 in Chicago and 5.3 in Phoenix, by NASA's averages ( solar panels in winter ). So a refill from empty can take more than one day, and a station that powers a fridge needs
 enough panel watts to put back what the fridge uses each day; each setup page works that out.
 Why a station may not charge from solar
 Too little voltage. One small panel on an input that starts at 30 V or more, or shade and low sun, can keep the panels below the input's lowest voltage.
 Too much voltage. Above the input's top voltage the station protects itself and stops, or is damaged. Recheck series strings in the cold.
 Too cold or too hot to charge. Most makers rate charging only from 0 °C (32 °F) upward; the manual gives the station's own range.
 A loose plug. An MC4 joint not clicked home, or an adapter cable made for another station's input.
 Questions buyers ask
 Do I need a separate charge controller? No, for the stations we list: each has a solar charge controller built in, which takes what the panels give up to the input's limits. Plug the panels into the input the maker names for solar.
 Can I use another brand's panels? Yes, when the voltage, current and watts stay inside the input's limits and you have the cable for the plugs. On 84 of the 119 stations we have setups for, the quickest maker panel on sale is another brand's. Some makers advise against mixing their panels with other brands or types in one array.
 Can I mix different panels in one array? It is best not to. In series, the panel with the lowest current holds back the string; in parallel, the strings settle at the lower voltage. Our setups use identical panels for that reason.
 Is a bigger panel always faster? Only up to the input's watt limit. A 400 W panel on a 200 W input charges at 200 W at most; it helps only by holding the limit for more of the day, at a higher price and weight.

How Long to Charge a Power Station with Solar? Maths 
 How long a power station takes to charge with solar
 Pinned models: EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus (US), Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 (US), Jackery SolarSaga 200W, Anker SOLIX C1000 (US) · Last checked 2026-10-28 · Last updated 2026-11-02 · How we research 
 Affiliate links. As an Amazon Associate we earn from qualifying purchases. Disclosure 
 Jump to a section Step 1: the station's limits 
 Step 2: what panels really deliver 
 Worked example 
 Why your solar input reads low 
 Choosing a setup 
 Sources 
 Checked: 2026-10-28. 
 Charge time (hours) ≈ watt-hours to add ÷ watts actually reaching the station. You get "watts actually reaching the station" by taking the panels' rated watts, capping them at the station's solar input limit, and then reducing them for real sunlight. Rated watts are a lab figure, so real charging is slower than the sum on the box.
 Step 1: the station's limits
 The station takes only as much solar power as its input allows, however many panels you connect.
 Station Capacity Solar input (manufacturer) Fastest possible (capacity ÷ max input) 
 EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus 1024 Wh 2 × 500 W MPPT (1000 W total) ≈ 1.0 h 
 Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 1070 Wh 2 × DC8mm, 16–60 V at 10.5 A, 400 W max total ≈ 2.7 h 
 Anker SOLIX C1000 1056 Wh 600 W max, 11–60 V ≈ 1.8 h 
 These are floors under perfect conditions. EcoFlow quotes a full charge in 70 minutes with 500 W × 2 of solar input. That's longer than the simple division gives, because charging slows as the battery fills.
 Step 2: what panels really deliver
 Panel ratings are measured at Standard Test Conditions (STC) : 1000 W/m² of sunlight with the cells at 25 °C. The Jackery SolarSaga 200W specification lists exactly these conditions. Jackery's own FAQ explains that the 200 W figure "is tested in an ideal laboratory", and that light intensity, panel angle and shade reduce what you see on the display.
 So think in peak sun hours : the number of hours of STC-strength sunlight your site gets in a day. A panel rated P watts yields at most about P × peak sun hours watt-hours per day, before conversion losses. Peak sun hours vary with location, season and weather, so look up a local figure and treat it as an estimate.
 Worked example
 Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 (1070 Wh) with one SolarSaga 200W panel:
 Rated input: 200 W, well under the 400 W limit.
 Ideal hours: 1070 ÷ 200 ≈ 5.4 hours of STC sunlight .
 With 4 peak sun hours a day (an illustrative figure, not a forecast), that's about 1.3 days of sun. With losses, it's more.
 With two panels (400 W), the ideal figure halves to about 2.7 hours, and you're at the station's 400 W cap. A third panel wouldn't speed things up. Before wiring panels together, check the voltage and current rules in series vs parallel wiring and panel pairing and Voc .
 Why your solar input reads low
 Angle and shade: Jackery names these as the main causes. Even part of a panel in shade lowers output.
 Weak light: cloud, haze, and low winter sun.
 Heat: the SolarSaga 200W spec gives a power temperature coefficient of −0.33 %/°C, so hot panels deliver less.
 Input limits: current above the per-port amp rating, or voltage outside the input window, is clipped or not accepted.
 Full battery: charging tapers near 100%.
 Choosing a setup
 To size the battery first, see how to size a power station . To compare the solar inputs of three ~1 kWh units side by side, see the DELTA 3 Plus vs Explorer 1000 v2 vs SOLIX C1000 comparison .
 Check EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus on Amazon (affiliate link) Check Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 on Amazon (affiliate link) Check Anker SOLIX C1000 on Amazon (affiliate link) 
 Related: panel pairing and Voc ; series or parallel wiring ; size a power station ; all solar guides ; off-grid EV charging from solar .
 Charging an EV from solar? See our guides for the US (120/240 V) and the EU, UK and Australia (230 V) for why a power station alone is not enough.

 Two Power Stations Hold the Same 1 kWh, So Where Do They Differ?
 Published September 23, 2026 · By the SolarPanelX editors · Prices and specs as of that date, from the pages under Sources
 Summary
 At the same capacity, the gaps show up in port output and in how many solar inputs there are. EcoFlow's DELTA 3 and DELTA 3 Plus both store 1,024 Wh and deliver 1,800 W AC, yet USB-C tops out at 100 W on one and 140 W on the other, and the Plus has two 500 W solar inputs instead of one, which EcoFlow says refills it from sunlight in about 70 minutes.
 Solar input is where the Plus pulls ahead
 Each DELTA model accepts 11 to 60 V at up to 500 W per solar input. DELTA 3 has one input; the Plus has two, and EcoFlow rates it at a full charge in 70 minutes with both in use. On DELTA 3, a larger array still enters at 500 W at most. Jackery's Explorer 1000 v2, a slightly larger 1,070 Wh unit, takes up to 400 W across its two DC inputs.
